summary: Learners discover Earth's layered interior by reasoning from seismic-wave evidence, treating the S-wave shadow zone as positive evidence of a liquid outer core. The core objective is indirect inference ('we cannot dig to the core, so how do we KNOW?'), not wave vocabulary. Learners first embody the two body-wave types physically, then simulate a quake, place seismometers worldwide, read arrivals, and reconstruct the four-layer model (crust, solid mantle, liquid outer core, solid inner core) step by step from P-first arrivals, refraction, the S shadow zone, and inner-core reflections.
misconceptions: 'S waves are just slower P waves.' — They are a different KIND of motion (shear/transverse vs compression/longitudinal); S being blocked by liquid is about wave type, not speed.

'The shadow zone means the waves were absorbed/used up.' — S waves are stopped because the liquid outer core cannot carry shear; P waves are refracted (bent) away, not destroyed — they reappear elsewhere.
'Seismic waves only travel along the surface.' — Body waves (P and S) travel THROUGH the Earth's interior; that through-travel is exactly what probes the layers.

'We know Earth's interior by drilling/sampling it.' — The deepest boreholes barely scratch the crust; the layered model is inferred almost entirely from seismic waves (plus meteorites, density, magnetism).
'The whole core is liquid' or 'the whole core is solid.' — The OUTER core is liquid (stops S), the INNER core is solid (revealed by reflected phases); conflating them loses the key evidence.
'A liquid outer core means a hollow or molten-through Earth.' — It is dense liquid iron–nickel under immense pressure, surrounded by solid mantle and a solid inner core, not a cavity or a lava sea.

activities.title: Feel the two kinds of wave: slinky (P) and shaken rope (S)
steps: Push and pull one end of a stretched slinky along its length and watch the compression pulse travel through: this is a longitudinal P-wave (push-pull along the direction of travel).
Shake a rope or spring side to side and watch the sideways ripple travel along it: this is a transverse S-wave (side-to-side shearing across the direction of travel).
State in your own words how the two motions differ, and predict which type needs a material that resists being bent/sheared sideways.
activities.insight: P-waves are compression (push-pull) and S-waves are shear (side-to-side) — a difference of KIND of motion, not just speed. Shear motion requires a material that resists change of shape.

activities.title: Fire a quake and ring the globe with seismometers
steps: On a cross-section of the Earth, place an earthquake focus and send P and S waves outward in all directions; watch P arrive first (it travels faster) and the rays bend (refract) at layer boundaries.

Place seismometer stations all around the globe and read each trace, colour-coding stations where both P and S arrive (e.g. green), stations where P arrives but no direct S does (e.g. yellow), and stations where neither direct P nor direct S arrives (e.g. grey, roughly 104°–140° from the quake), to make the pattern visible.

Find all the far-side stations (beyond about 104° from the quake) that never record any direct S, and write down exactly what is present and what is absent there, noting where P is still recorded (beyond about 140°) and where direct P is also missing (about 104°–140°).
activities.insight: From the SAME earthquake, no station beyond about 104° from the quake records direct S, yet P still reaches many of those far-side stations (beyond about 140°), so the missing S cannot be explained by distance or fading. A separate, narrower P shadow zone (about 104°–140°) appears because P-waves are bent (refracted) at the core boundary, not stopped.

activities.title: Test the shadow zone: toggle the outer core solid vs liquid
steps: Switch the outer core from solid to liquid and back, and watch what happens to the S-waves at that boundary and to the far-side shadow band.
Record: with a liquid outer core, S-waves stop at the boundary and a far-side shadow zone appears; with a solid outer core, S-waves pass through and the S shadow zone disappears.
Reason backwards from the real data (an S shadow zone exists) to the conclusion: the outer core must be liquid, because only a liquid stops shear waves.
activities.insight: The ABSENCE of S on the far side is itself the evidence — it means shear waves hit a liquid layer. The shadow zone is a positive clue, not missing information.

activities.title: Reconstruct Earth's four layers from the data alone
steps: With the cutaway hidden, use only the pattern of what arrived where and when to rebuild Earth's structure layer by layer: P-first arrivals, refraction/travel-time bending, the S shadow zone, then a faint reflected phase.

Identify the mantle as solid (S-waves DO cross it), the outer core as liquid (S shadow zone), and the inner core as a separate region (its boundary is revealed by waves reflecting or refracting off it inside the liquid outer core), which further evidence, such as P-waves speeding up inside it, shows is solid.
Write a short explanation of how each clue pins down each layer, then compare your inferred model with the actual layered Earth.
Predict: what would far-side seismometers detect if the outer core were solid, and how is the solid inner core detected despite sitting inside a liquid?
activities.insight: The whole layered model (crust / solid mantle / liquid outer core / solid inner core) is reconstructed from indirect wave evidence, built up clue by clue — we map the unreachable interior by reasoning, not by digging.

activities.title: The detective story: discovering the inner core
steps: Read or listen to a short account of how seismologists read wiggly seismograph traces to deduce the interior, including how Inge Lehmann (1936) inferred an inner core from faint P-wave arrivals inside the P-wave shadow zone, and how later evidence showed that inner core is solid.
Discuss what made each discovery possible: which absence or faint arrival carried the information.
Explain why this counts as science even though no one has ever been to the core.
activities.insight: Scientific knowledge of the unreachable interior is built from indirect, often subtle signals — including absences and faint reflections — and refined over time.

checkQuestion: On the far side of the Earth from a big earthquake, seismometers detect P-waves but no S-waves at all. What does this missing signal tell us about what is deep inside the Earth, and why?
checkAnswer: S-waves are shear waves that cannot travel through liquid; P-waves travel through both solid and liquid. The S-waves vanishing on the far side (the S-wave shadow zone) means they hit something liquid and were stopped — that is the evidence for a LIQUID outer core. The absence of the signal is itself the clue: nobody has drilled there, so we infer the interior indirectly from how the waves behave.
